title: Strip 10 mm of insulation off a cable end in a lever-operated benchtop stripping station
instruction: Strip 10 mm of insulation off the cable's free end in the stripping station, then let the station's lever back up and take your hands off it.
context: Stripping cable ends to a set length is regular work in electrical installation and assembly: for electricians (about 821,000 US jobs in 2025 per BLS, wire strippers among their everyday tools), who strip every conductor they "Connect ... to circuit breakers, transformers, or other components" (O*NET), and for electrical and electronic equipment assemblers (246,300) and team assemblers (1,403,500; O*NET: "Provide assistance in the production of wiring assemblies") building panels and harnesses. Too short and the terminal does not seat; too long and bare copper shows. A benchtop stripper's blades only stay shut while its lever is held down, and the cut insulation only comes off if the cable is pulled out while they are shut.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A fixed steel wire-stripping station, 0.65 kg, its bore's axis 24 cm forward and 12 cm left of the centre line: a block 5 x 5 cm and 3 cm tall with a funnel on top, 44 mm across at its rim (4 cm above the table), narrowing to a 12 mm throat at the block's top face; below, a bore 16 mm across down to a floor 5 mm above the table. At the throat two opposed full-radius V-blades of hardened tool steel (1.0 mm thick, edges ground to 20 degrees, each notch a 90-degree V ending in a semicircle 3.95 mm in radius) slide toward each other along the lever's direction, symmetric about the bore's axis (a rack and pinion keeps them centred): open, a 12.0 mm opening (0.85 mm all round the 10.3 mm cable); closed, a 7.9 mm circle, the conductor's diameter, cutting the 1.2 mm insulation all round. An eccentric on the lever's hub, 13.06 mm off the hinge axis, drives the right blade carrier through a slot and swings from 10 degrees before to 10 degrees past straight down over the lever's 20 degrees: each blade moves 4.54 mm (the grip 69.8 mm), meeting the insulation 14.5 degrees from closed. The lever, a steel tube 24 x 16 mm with 1 mm walls, 24.5 cm long (2 cm behind the hinge, 22.5 cm in front), with a red rubber grip sleeve 5 cm long centred 20 cm from the hinge, 163 g, is hinged 5.2 cm above the table and 3 cm right of the bore's axis and reaches right (its grip 11 cm right of the centre line when closed). A torsion spring of 0.04 N m per degree, wound 10 degrees (0.40 N m) on the open stop, holds it 20 degrees up (the grip 6.8 cm above where it closes); closed it gives 0.40 + 0.04 x 20 = 1.20 N m, less 0.18 N m from the lever's weight: 5.1 N at the grip. With a cable in, the cut adds up to 2.91 N m (14.6 N at the grip, 19.7 N in all; computed for PVC of 12.5 N/mm2 tensile strength). Closed, the blades sit in the cut, so the cut sleeve bears on their undersides as the cable is pulled out (about 20 N, the sleeve's friction on the conductor) and then drops onto the bore's floor. (2) A loose single-core cable of type H07V-K 1 x 35 mm2 (a manufacturer's datasheet: a 35 mm2 class 5 flexible copper conductor 7.9 mm across, under 1.2 mm of PVC insulation, 10.3 mm across overall, 340 g per metre; EN 50525-2-31 allows up to 11.7 mm overall), 12 cm long, its top 3 cm moulded into a square grey ABS plug (16 mm, 3 cm tall), 46.2 g in all (40.8 g of cable, 0.12 m x 340 g/m, and the plug's 5.4 g of ABS); at its free end 24 mm of insulation covers the core. It stands upright, plug up, with its free end in a small black ABS holder 30 cm forward and 21 cm left of the centre line: a cup with a 12 mm bore (0.85 mm of clearance all round the 10.3 mm cable, and wider than the 11.7 mm maximum), 2 mm walls up to 1.8 cm above the table and a base 20 mm across and 4 mm thick, on which the cable's end stands. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. The cut: when the lever first closes (within 0.5 degrees of its stop) with the cable's end below the blades, the insulation between the end and the blades is cut, to the nearest 2 mm, and the closed blades hold the cable until it is pulled with 20 N. Stripped: the cable then pulled out (its end 2 mm above the blades) while the lever is still down (within 4 degrees of closed, where the blades still cover 1.1 mm of the cut sleeve's 1.2 mm wall); if the lever comes up first, the cut insulation stays on the cable. Released: the lever back up at least 15 degrees and both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) at least 4 cm from its grip. 1.0: 8 to 12 mm stripped, released; 0.5: any strip, or a cut of 8 to 12 mm with the blades still closed on it; 0.25: the cable's end at least 5 mm below the blades at some point; else 0.0. In a real trial the stripped length is measured with a caliper from the conductor's end to the insulation's cut edge (8 to 12 mm for 1.0), the cut sleeve is found on the bore's floor, and the insertion, the order of pull and lever and the release are judged from the overhead video; before trials a force gauge checks that closing the lever on a cable end peaks at 15 to 25 N at the grip and that pulling a cut cable out takes 15 to 25 N. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the lever and the cable still for 1 s.
reset_notes: Unscrew the bore's floor plug and empty the cut insulation out of the station, stand a fresh cable in the holder, plug up, and let the lever spring up.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 20 Hz control) at real size and mass; the cable is stiff. Simplified: the blades are not bodies. With the cable in, the closing lever meets the computed cutting torque (to 2.91 N m); once closed, the insulation below the blades (12 shown 2 mm rings, one collision cylinder) is cut to the nearest 2 mm and held by the station, and a joint that breaks at 20 N holds the cable. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
